# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1–13 (Complete – Updated 110)

## Setting and Time
- **Current Period**: Spring of fourth year in Mirecombe hill farms (Seena with aching back; Ellan Lindner humming childhood tune; Maric counting coins; son Isnar Brackwood born). Earlier: Winter of third year with frost on hedges. Evening at Brighton following Dobbin's arrival. Fine brilliant moonlight night of May. Army ordered to Belgium; embarkation completed two days after Mrs. O'Dowd's party. Transports proceeded under convoy to Ostend with band playing "God Save the King." Amelia and Jos proceeded to Ramsgate for passage to Ostend. **Current Status**: All now in Belgium, beginning "happy time" with military festival, churches, galleries, rides, opera; greatest event of history (Waterloo campaign) pending; opening summer of 1815; Napoleon screened behind frontier-fortresses preparing outbreak.
- **Primary Locations**: London (Russell Square, Thames Street counting-house, Slaughters' hotel, Gray's Inn Square, Hulker and Bullock bankers on Lombard Street), Brighton (George-Amelia honeymoon, Rawdon-Rebecca residence, Ship Inn, beach), Mirecombe (Seena Orlwood—drowned in flood; Pebin Wexwood, Maric Lindson, Rozek Hollwood, Halan Hollwood, Isbin Hollwood, Orvie, Nynelle Stenworth, Seena Hollett, Brenelle and Orvie Hollett, Thidrek Corrett, Feten Lindner, Old Maric, Ilena Orlwood, Orrine, Staveton; river crossing at Gulton with frost-silvered hedges), Chatham (embarkation point, 150th regiment mess, Mrs. O'Dowd's apartments), Harwich, Fulham (Mrs. Sedley's house, Mr. and Mrs. Clapp, Miss Flannigan), Ramsgate, Ostend, Brussels (Hotel de Ville, flower-market, Park, restaurateur's establishment, general's party venue), Belgium (flat, flourishing country with green fields, quiet cities, chaussees, canal-boats, rich pastures, pleasant villages, old chateaux; Bruges market; crowded with well-to-do English travellers; Highlanders billeted in Flemish farm-houses).

## Main Characters

**Captain William Dobbin** [MAJOR CHARACTER]
- **Actions - COMPLETED**: Arrived Brighton via Slaughters' hotel; witnessed Stubble's tears; dined with officers. At Ship Inn: assumed jovial manner hiding feelings upon seeing Amelia; made clumsy compliments. In George's room: delivered disinheritance letter; George erupted; Dobbin offered financial support, promised not to forget godson; George forgave him. Evening dinner: described Belgium fetes and fashion; flushed red when Rebecca announced intention to go to Belgium, objected about danger, became confused and silent. At Cavendish Square Hotel: attempted remonstrance against extravagance; George dismissed concerns. Walked home musing. At Chatham: wore shells on frockcoat, crimson sash and sabre; paced street in expectation; presented military appearance. Recognized Amelia upon arrival. Never spoke to Amelia during Mrs. O'Dowd's party; took Jos home (maudlin state); handed Amelia into carriage as she departed; she rebuked him smilingly for ignoring her; loitered smoking cigar afterward watching lights from George's windows; did not return to quarters until almost morning. Bought piano for Amelia's father's house at Fulham. **Currently in Belgium with regiment**.
- **In Belgium - NEW**: Captain Dobbin "in a rage" at behaviour of Lady Blanche Thistlewood and Countess of Bareacres toward Amelia at George's dinner party.
- **Internal Conflict**: Deeply troubled by guilt over hastening marriage; feels his unendurable suspense drove him to crush uncertainty; considers himself traitor to both father and son. Secret adoration of Amelia is his "greatest privilege and hope of life"; privately resolved he would not have let her go to Belgium if married to her. Knows Amelia considers him plain, awkward, ungainly; acquiesces humbly.
- **Reputation**: "Greatly respected in the regiment, as the best officer and the cleverest man in it"

**George Osborne** [MAJOR CHARACTER]
- **Status - MARRIED, DISINHERITED**: Married Amelia late April without father's consent; honeymoon at Brighton; disinherited by lawyer letter (determination "final and irrevocable"). Receives £2,000 in 4 percent annuities and £100/year widow's allowance for Amelia.
- **Financial Crisis**: Lost £140 to Rawdon Crawley at cards; gave substantial payment from bank-notes and bill on agents. Hotel bill and card losses nearly drained purse. Obtained £2,000 cheque from Hulker and Bullock bankers. Fred Bullock (cadaverous suitor of George's sister Jane) turned deadly colour and slunk away upon seeing George at bankers. At Chatham: sent Amelia once more to her mother with strict orders and carte blanche to purchase everything requisite for lady of Mrs. George Osborne's fashion. Paid with cheques "with the splendour of a lord." Highly pleased with day's business.
- **In Belgium - NEW**: **Ashamed of regiment company and resolved to exchange into better regiment soon and get wife away from "damned vulgar women"** (though Amelia herself remains unaffected and unembarrassed). Takes wife to new jaunt or junket every night; quite pleased with himself; swears becoming domestic character. Sight of great company of lords, ladies, and fashionable persons fills his truly British soul with intense delight. **Had honour of dancing with Lady Blanche Thistlewood, Lord Bareacres' daughter; bustled for ices and refreshments; pushed and squeezed for carriage; bragged about Countess at home in way old father could not have surpassed.** Called upon ladies next day; rode by their side in Park; asked their party to great dinner at restaurateur's; wild with exultation when they agreed to come. **Spent great deal of money on this festival entertainment**. Mrs. Sedley in London mightily pleased and talked about Emmy's friend the Countess with such assiduity that news of son entertaining peers and peeresses came to Osborne's ears in the City.
- **Expectations and Character**: Believes father will relent before long. Determines to distinguish himself prodigiously in campaign so old gentleman must give in. Reflects "the world was before him" and luck might change at cards.

**Amelia Osborne** [MAJOR CHARACTER]
- **Actions - COMPLETED**: Troubled by Rebecca's wit; misgings about Rebecca; tormented by guilt about forcing marriage and causing disinheritance. Face cleared reading disinheritance letter. Cried with "greatest spirit" determination to accompany George to Belgium. Rose early; packed trunks with "greatest alacrity" while George lay in bed. Made "little disappointed curtsey" when George declined accompanying her to Fulham. Mother clasped her to heart with "all maternal eagerness and affection," ran out weeping; old Mr. Clapp alarmed in shirt-sleeves; Irish servant-lass rushed up smiling "God bless you." Upstairs to little room: sank into chair; fell to thinking over past week; reflected on Rebecca's "twinkling green eyes and baleful smile"; indulged in selfish brooding and listless melancholy; thought with terror of funereal damask pavilion at grand hotel; knelt by bedside seeking spiritual consolation. When tea announced, came downstairs "a great deal more cheerful"; kissed father and mother; talked to old gentleman making him more merry than many a day; sat at piano (purchased by Dobbin) and sang all his favourite old songs; praised tea and marmalade arrangement; finding herself so by determining to make everybody else happy; was sound asleep in pavilion; woke with smile when George arrived from theatre. Bustling about from milliner to linen-draper completing outfit with great taste and elegant discernment; Mrs. Sedley sincerely happy for first time since misfortunes.
- **At Mrs. O'Dowd's Party - COMPLETED**: Recognized lady as one George often laughed about. Grasped Amelia's hand very warmly. Being quiet, good-natured, and not too handsome, made agreeable impression until gentlemen arrived, who all admired her so sisters began to find fault. Had "little triumph" which flushed spirits and made eyes sparkle. Resolved: "I will make all his friends welcome. I will love all as I love him. I will always try and be gay and good-humoured and make his home happy." Adopted by regiment with acclamation. Captains approved, Lieutenants applauded, Ensigns admired. Old Cutler made professional jokes; Cackle examined her upon literature and three best French quotations. Young Stubble whispering "Jove, isn't she a pretty gal?" and never took eyes off her except when negus came. Gave Dobbin her little hand departing party; rebuked him smilingly for ignoring her all night.
- **In Belgium - NEW**: **A natural and unaffected person with none of artificial shamefacedness; only amused by Mrs. O'Dowd's honest eccentricities, not in least ashamed of her company.** Letters home to mother filled with delight and gratitude. Husband bade her buy laces, millinery, jewels, gimcracks; he was kindest, best, most generous of men. **Thought about her husband and how best to show her love for him amid great topics of world.** Every day during happy time brought novelty and amusement. **At general's party given for George's regiment division: Countess of Bareacres would not answer when spoken to; Lady Blanche stared with eye-glass; Amelia wrote most piteous accounts home; told how rudeness and her own discomfiture made her uncomfortable; ladies carefully excluded her from conversation.** Yet she wrote home regarding guests' rudeness and her discomfiture, and old Mrs. Sedley was mightily pleased nevertheless.

**Mrs. Major Peggy O'Dowd** [MAJOR CHARACTER]
- One of five sisters and eleven children of noble house of Glenmalony; ordered cousin Mick O'Dowd to marry her when about thirty-three after trying nine seasons at Dublin and two at Bath and Cheltenham. Mick obeyed and carried her to West Indies.
- **At Mrs. O'Dowd's Party - COMPLETED**: Sent Amelia triangular billet on pink paper sealed with dove and olive branch; received her warmly with great vivacity. Told of her birth and pedigree; expressed intention that Glorvina would have suited George; determined to take Amelia as sister and love her as one of family; assured they would agree. Dispatched Ensign Simple to Colonel Tavish about Jos. Remarked: "Hould your tongue, Mick, you booby. Them husbands are always in the way"; warned Mick about propriety. Introduced Jos to herself and Mick. Gossiped at tea-time about George's reformed rake status and Amelia's position as wife. Inquired about Mrs. Kirk's evangelical questions; presented penny books: "Howling Wilderness," "Washerwoman of Wandsworth Common," "British Soldier's best Bayonet." Assisted Jos in learning military names with great assiduity.
- **In Belgium - NEW**: Traveling with Amelia and Jos as one of "most entertaining" companions; continually prattles about Ballinasloe canal-boats, Dublin cattle (father's gold medal heifer), comparison of markets, Ballinafad, Glenmalony stables, claret drunk there. Remarked about flowers: "You should see the flowers at Glenmalony. Me fawther has three Scotch garners with nine helpers. We have an acre of hot-houses, and pines as common as pays in the sayson. Our greeps weighs six pounds every bunch of 'em, and upon me honour and conscience I think our magnolias is as big as taykettles." Cock's plume in hat and very large repayther on stomach which she rings on all occasions, narrating it presented by her fawther as she stept into carriage after marriage; these ornaments and other peculiarities give excruciating agonies to Captain Osborne when wives in contact; Amelia only amused by honest lady's eccentricities.

**Major Mick O'Dowd** [MINOR CHARACTER]
- Served sovereign in every quarter of world; paid for every step by acts of daring and gallantry. Most modest, silent, sheep-faced, meek of little men; obedient to wife as if tay-boy. At mess-table sits silently and drinks great deal; when full of liquor, reels silently home. Speaks only to agree with everybody on every point; passes through life in perfect ease and good-humour. Never heated temper in hottest suns of India; never shaken by Walcheren ague. Walked up to battery with same indifference as to dinner-table; dined on horse-flesh and turtle with equal relish. Had old mother, Mrs. O'Dowd of O'Dowdstown; never disobeyed except when enlisted and when persisted in marrying "that odious Peggy Malony."

**Jos Sedley** [MAJOR CHARACTER]
- **Actions - COMPLETED**: Arrived Chatham in fine carriage with Amelia. Recognized friendly countenance of Captain Dobbin. Attended Mrs. O'Dowd's party in maudlin state; told tiger-hunt story with great effect at mess-table and soiree to Mrs. O'Dowd in her turban and bird of paradise. Dobbin and Captain Porter took him home to hotel. Agreed to escort Amelia and Mrs. O'Dowd abroad. Ceased shaving upper lip upon agreeing. Followed parades and drills with great assiduity at Chatham; listened with utmost attention to "brother officers." Received excellent assistance from Mrs. O'Dowd in military studies. Made appearance in braided frock-coat and duck trousers, foraging cap with smart gold band. Had carriage; informed everybody on board Lovely Rose confidentially he was joining Duke of Wellington's army; folks mistook him for commissary-general or government courier. Courage prodigious; cried "Boney attack us!"; assured "poor Emmy" of no danger; explained allied military superiority with knowledge of three hundred thousand Russians under Wittgenstein and Barclay de Tolly, five hundred thousand Austrians under Schwartzenberg and Prince Charles, Prussians under Prince Marshal. Treated young officers with sumptuosity; amusing them by military airs. **In Belgium - NEW**: Interposed about curry and rice at Dumdum during Belgium journey; owned with sigh that for good streaky beef mingled with fat and lean, there was no country like England (despite Mrs. O'Dowd's patriotic assertions about Irish beef).

**John Osborne (Old Mr. Osborne)** [MAJOR CHARACTER]
- Wealthy merchant; George's father; savage, determined man. Upon learning George married Amelia, erupted in fury. Retreated to study; locked door; retrieved mahogany escritoire; examined George's documents with "curses quivering on livid lips" and "horrid hatred and disappointment"; marked, docketed, catalogued with dates. Commissioned lawyer to draft letter stating determination "final and irrevocable." George ceases to be family member; Money expended in minority exceeds entitlement; Osborne waives all claim upon George's estate. **In London, news how son is entertaining peers and peeresses actually came to Osborne's ears in the City.**

**Rebecca Sharp (Mrs. Rebecca Rawdon Crawley)** [MAJOR CHARACTER]
- Secretly married to Rawdon; heavily indebted. All reconciliation attempts with Miss Crawley permanently rebuffed; Miss Crawley refused Rebecca and Rawdon; sent Rawdon to lawyer with negative outcome; disparaged Rawdon's appearance and habits. Successfully reconciled with Miss Briggs on beach through letter-writing campaign; Miss Crawley recognized Rebecca's composition not Rawdon's and concluded "that little serpent of a governess who rules him." Monetary scheme executed: sent crumpled note to Rawdon requesting money from "Cupid" (George); Rawdon extracted considerable payment in bank-notes and bill on agents. Rebecca remarked: "A comfortable inn in Brighton is better than a spunging-house in Chancery Lane"; noted Jos and Captain Cupid are better companions than sheriff's officers. Packed chief valuables and sent them off under care of George's servant on coach to London. **Currently in London with Rawdon, not proceeding to Belgium.**

**Rawdon Crawley** [MAJOR CHARACTER]
- Secretly married to Rebecca; heavily indebted. Extracted considerable payment from George in bank-notes and bill on agents; lost £140 to George at cards. Met Miss Crawley when she took air in chair; she held out couple of fingers; Rawdon turned red as scarlet with rapture and confusion. Miss Crawley subsequently disparaged his appearance, character, and drinking. Visited Miss Crawley's lawyer in Gray's Inn Square; "came back furious" to Rebecca. **Currently in London, not proceeding to Belgium.**

## Critical Facts and Status

- **MILITARY CAMPAIGN - UNDERWAY IN BELGIUM**: Regiment departed Chatham two days after Mrs. O'Dowd's party; transports proceeded under convoy to Ostend with band playing "God Save the King"; appeared brilliant and harmless as Hyde Park review; soldiers paid scores at village inns; Highlanders billeted in Flemish farm-houses. Amelia, Jos, and Mrs. O'Dowd drove unencumbered to Ramsgate and had speedy passage to Ostend on packets. All now in Belgium enjoying "happy time" with military festival, churches, galleries, rides, opera; English bugles wake soldiers each morning; at nightfall British fife and drum; greatest event of history (Napoleon outbreak) pending; European continent in arms.
- **GEORGE-AMELIA MARRIAGE - ESTABLISHED, EMOTIONALLY SECURE**: Married late April; disinheritance "final and irrevocable"; obtained £2,000 cheque; George now ashamed of regiment company but resolved to exchange soon. Amelia emotionally stable, grateful, loves George deeply, received triumph at Mrs. O'Dowd's party. Both in Belgium; George takes her to nightly jaunts and junkets; Amelia sends delighted letters home despite rudeness from Lady Blanche and Countess of Bareacres at George's dinner party (whom he paid considerable sums to entertain).
- **REBECCA-RAWDON STATUS - LONDON-BASED, ISOLATED**: Miss Crawley reconciliation permanently failed; both now in London; Rawdon furious after lawyer visit; not proceeding to Belgium; financial situation acute and ongoing.
